title: HCF and LCM Grade 5: Listing, Prime Factorisation & Word Problems + Free Quiz

meta_desc: Learn HCF and LCM for Grade 5 by listing and prime factorisation, plus how to tell which one a word problem needs. Free quiz and printable practice.
excerpt: The hard part of HCF and LCM at Grade 5 is not the maths — it is knowing which one a word problem is asking for. Here is how I teach both methods and, more importantly, how to choose the right one.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Give a Grade 5 class the sum ‘find the HCF and LCM of 12 and 18’ and most will grind through it fine. Wrap the same numbers in a story — ‘two ribbons of 12 cm and 18 cm, cut into equal pieces with none left over, what is the longest each piece can be?’ — and half the hands go down. That gap is the whole game. HCF and LCM at Grade 5 are not really about the arithmetic; they are about reading a problem and knowing which of the two you actually need.

So this guide does two things. First, the mechanics: finding HCF (highest common factor) and LCM (lowest common multiple) two ways — by listing and by prime factorisation. Then the part textbooks rush: a plain-English test for deciding, from the words alone, whether a question wants HCF or LCM.

What HCF and LCM actually mean

Strip away the jargon and both ideas are small. The HCF of two numbers is the biggest number that divides into both of them exactly. The LCM is the smallest number that both of them divide into exactly. One looks down at what the numbers share; the other looks up at where they next meet.

I tell students to hear it in the names. Highest common factor — a factor is something that fits inside, so HCF is the biggest thing that fits inside both. Lowest common multiple — a multiple is a number in the times-table, so LCM is the first place both times-tables land on the same number.

Method 1: finding HCF and LCM by listing

Listing is slow but it never lies, and for small numbers it builds real understanding. For the HCF, write out the factors of each number and ring the biggest one they share.

  • Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12
  • Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18
  • Common factors: 1, 2, 3, 6 — so the HCF is 6.

For the LCM, list the multiples (the times-table) of each and find the first one that appears in both lists.

  • Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24…
  • Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24…
  • First shared multiple: 12 — so the LCM is 12.

Listing works beautifully up to about 20. Past that the lists get long and someone always misses a factor, which is exactly when prime factorisation earns its place.

Method 2: finding HCF and LCM by prime factorisation

This is the method that scales. Break each number into a product of primes using a factor tree, then apply two short rules.

Take 24 and 36. As primes, 24 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 and 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3.

  • HCF — multiply only the primes both numbers share: they share 2, 2 and 3, so HCF = 2 × 2 × 3 = 12.
  • LCM — take every prime, using the highest count in either number: three 2s (from 24) and two 3s (from 36), so LCM = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 = 72.

Here is a check worth teaching, because it catches almost every slip: HCF × LCM should equal the two numbers multiplied together. 12 × 72 = 864, and 24 × 36 = 864. They match, so the answer stands. A wrong HCF or LCM breaks this instantly.

The real skill: which one does the word problem want?

This is where marks are won and lost, so it deserves the most attention. Almost every Grade 5 word problem falls into one of two shapes, and the story tells you which.

Reach for HCF when you are splitting things into the biggest equal groups — cutting, sharing or arranging into the largest identical batches with nothing left over. Reach for LCM when you are asking when repeating events line up again — two things that happen on their own cycle and you want the next time they happen together.

The story is about…You needTypical clue words
Cutting or sharing into the biggest equal partsHCFlargest, greatest, maximum, equal groups
Events repeating and meeting againLCMnext time, again together, smallest number
Ribbon of 12 cm and 18 cm, longest equal piecesHCF (= 6 cm)‘longest’ points down
Bells ringing every 4 and 6 minutes, next togetherLCM (= 12 min)‘next together’ points up

My one shortcut for anxious students: if the answer must be smaller than the numbers you started with (a piece cut from a length), it is HCF. If the answer must be bigger (a later time, a larger quantity), it is LCM. It is not a law of mathematics, but for Grade 5 word problems it is right often enough to be a genuine lifeline.

A worked word problem, start to finish

‘Anaya has 24 blue beads and 36 red beads. She wants to make identical bracelets using all the beads, with the same number of blue and the same number of red on each. What is the greatest number of bracelets she can make?’

The story splits beads into equal groups, and it asks for the greatest number — that is HCF. The HCF of 24 and 36 is 12, so Anaya can make 12 identical bracelets. Notice the answer is smaller than both numbers, exactly as the shortcut predicts.

quiz.title: HCF and LCM Grade 5 Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on finding HCF and LCM by listing and prime factorisation, plus choosing the right one in word problems. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: What is the HCF of 12 and 18?
questions.explanation: Common factors of 12 and 18 are 1, 2, 3 and 6. The highest is 6.

questions.q: What is the LCM of 4 and 6?
questions.explanation: Multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12… and of 6 are 6, 12… The first shared one is 12.

questions.q: Using primes, 24 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 and 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. What is their HCF?
What is the LCM of 24 and 36?
questions.explanation: Take the highest count of each prime: three 2s and two 3s give 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 = 72.

questions.q: Two ribbons, 12 cm and 18 cm, are cut into equal pieces with none left over. What is the longest each piece can be?
questions.explanation: The longest equal piece means HCF. The HCF of 12 and 18 is 6 cm.

questions.q: Two bells ring every 4 minutes and every 6 minutes. If they ring together now, when do they next ring together?
questions.explanation: ‘Next together’ means LCM. The LCM of 4 and 6 is 12 minutes.

questions.q: Which words in a problem usually point to LCM?
questions.explanation: LCM is about repeating events meeting again — ‘next time together’. The other options describe HCF.

questions.q: For 8 and 12, HCF = 4 and LCM = 24. Which check confirms this is correct?
questions.explanation: HCF × LCM equals the two numbers multiplied: 4 × 24 = 96 and 8 × 12 = 96.

faq.q: What is the difference between HCF and LCM in simple words?
faq.a: HCF is the biggest number that divides into both of your numbers, so it is always smaller than or equal to them. LCM is the smallest number that both of your numbers divide into, so it is always bigger than or equal to them. HCF looks down at what they share; LCM looks up at where they meet.

faq.q: Should a Grade 5 child use listing or prime factorisation?
faq.a: Both. Listing builds understanding and is quick for small numbers up to about 20. Prime factorisation is the method that keeps working for larger numbers, so teach listing first, then move on to factor trees once the idea is secure.

faq.q: How do I know if a word problem needs HCF or LCM?
faq.a: If the story splits things into the biggest equal groups — cutting, sharing, arranging with nothing left over — it is HCF. If it asks when repeating events line up again, it is LCM. A rough guide: if the answer is smaller than your numbers it is HCF; if larger, it is LCM.

faq.q: Is there a quick way to check an HCF and LCM answer?
faq.a: Yes. Multiply the HCF by the LCM — it should equal the two original numbers multiplied together. If they do not match, one of your answers is wrong, so it is worth doing every time.
